lead: Both readings correct a kind of pride. James tells the confident planners, who say they will go to this town and make this profit, that life is a mist and that every plan should be made under the words “If the Lord wishes”. In Luke, the disciples want to stop a man who is casting out demons in Jesus’ name because he is not one of their group, and later want fire to fall on a village that will not receive Jesus. Jesus answers both times with a correction and a wider heart. God is the Lord of our plans, and his grace is not confined by our boundaries.

set: James has just spoken against judging a neighbour (4:11–12). Now he turns to a different arrogance: the traveling merchant who plans a year of business as if the future were his own. The merchants of the Mediterranean world moved from city to city, and James knows the type. He does not condemn business or planning; he condemns planning that leaves God out.
str: v. 13: the planners: “today or tomorrow we will go…”.
v. 14: the reply: you do not know what tomorrow will bring; life is a mist.
v. 15: the right attitude: “If the Lord wishes…”.
vv. 16–17: boasting is evil; and the sin of knowing the good and not doing it.
kw: The word is used of smoke or of breath on a cold morning. Life is brief and cannot be held, a theme of Psalm 39:5–6 and Psalm 144:4.
A word for a show-off who claims more than he has. James calls it “evil”, not because it is loud but because it takes God’s place.
Verse 17 defines sin as failing to do the good one knows: sin of omission as well as of commission.
vv: Yet you do not even know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes.
A sober reminder. James is not gloomy; he wants us to live wisely, aware that each day is a gift.
Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wishes, we will live and do this or that.”
Not a mere formula to be recited, but a way of living: the plan is made, and held open to God’s will. Paul uses the same phrase (1 Corinthians 4:19; Acts 18:21).
As it is, you boast in your arrogance; all such boasting is evil.
Self-reliance that forgets God is not a small fault. James names it for what it is.
Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, commits sin.
A searching verse for the conscience: it is not enough to avoid doing wrong; we are also answerable for the good we leave undone.
ch: The Church teaches that God’s providence guides all things, and that Jesus asks us to abandon ourselves with childlike trust to the providence of the heavenly Father, who cares for the smallest needs of his children (CCC 305). The Catechism also teaches that sin may be committed by omission as well as by commission (CCC 1853). The words “If the Lord wishes” are not an excuse for idleness: they are the other side of the Our Father, “Your will be done”.

set: Luke 9 is the turning point of the Gospel. After Peter’s confession and the Transfiguration, “he set his face to go to Jerusalem” (9:51), and the long journey narrative begins, lasting to Luke 19:28. The two stories in today’s reading show how the disciples must learn on the road: John’s concern about an outside exorcist, and James and John’s anger at a Samaritan village.

Jews and Samaritans had been long divided, and many Jews travelling between Galilee and Jerusalem avoided Samaritan territory. The Samaritans worshipped on Mount Gerizim, so a party on its way to the Temple at Jerusalem touched an old disagreement. Luke will later make a Samaritan the model of neighbourly love (10:30–37; 17:11–19).
str: vv. 49–50: John reports an exorcist who does not follow with them; Jesus: “Do not stop him”.
v. 51: Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem, the days of his being “taken up” drawing near.
vv. 52–53: messengers to a Samaritan village; the village does not receive him.
vv. 54–56: James and John want fire from heaven; Jesus rebukes them; they go on.
kw: The word in v. 51 points beyond the Cross to the Ascension. Luke sees Jesus’ journey to Jerusalem as a journey to glory through death.
The same word appears for the exorcist (“casting out demons”) in v. 49. The unnamed man is doing the work Jesus himself does, in Jesus’ name.
Jesus uses the same word of rebuking evil spirits and storms. He rebukes his own disciples’ wish for vengeance as something to be driven out.
vv: we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.
The disciples’ reason: he does not belong to our group. They do not deny that the work is genuine.
Do not stop him; for whoever is not against you is for you.

Jesus refuses to draw the circle narrowly. Compare Mark 9:38–41. Elsewhere he says that whoever is not with him is against him (Luke 11:23): the two sayings together warn against both indifference and narrowness.
When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.
“Set his face” echoes Isaiah 50:7, the servant who sets his face like flint. He goes toward Jerusalem knowing what awaits him.
Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them?

The echo is of Elijah and the fire in 2 Kings 1:10–12. Some later manuscripts add “as Elijah did”, and, after v. 55, the words “You do not know what spirit you are of, for the Son of Man has not come to destroy the lives of people but to save them”. These additions are probably not original, but they express the sense of the story well.
But he turned and rebuked them.
Jesus turns and faces them. The prophet Elijah called down fire; the Son of Man refuses. His way is not destruction.
ch: The Church has seen in Jesus’ answer to John a call to recognise good wherever it is found: the Second Vatican Council teaches that many elements of sanctification and truth are found outside the visible structure of the Catholic Church, and that these, as gifts belonging to Christ’s Church, impel toward Catholic unity (Lumen Gentium 8; Unitatis Redintegratio 3). The refusal of fire teaches that the Gospel is never to be spread by force: no one is to be compelled to embrace the faith (Dignitatis Humanae 10).

qa: Does “whoever is not against you is for you” mean that all religions and Churches are the same?

No. Jesus is speaking about a man who casts out demons in his own name, and he teaches his disciples not to be jealous of good done in his name by someone outside their circle. The Church teaches that Christ founded one Church and that the fullness of the means of salvation subsists in the Catholic Church, while she rejoices in the grace and truth found in other Churches and treats others with respect (Lumen Gentium 8, 15; Nostra Aetate 2). Jealousy and violence are never the Church’s way.
study: James reminds us that we do not know what tomorrow will bring. What plan of mine do I need to hold more openly, saying “If the Lord wishes”?

The disciples wanted to stop someone who was not “one of us”, and to punish those who would not welcome Jesus. Where am I tempted to limit God’s work to my own group, or to answer rejection with anger?
